findings.title: Two-tier connection topology: gateway is a one-shot TCP redirect, all gameplay is direct client↔shard
findings.detail: The client connects to the gateway (TCP NodePort 30777 → host :7777) ONLY to send a single Connect message and receive a ShardRedirect; the gateway then closes. All actual gameplay (TCP control, UDP WorldState/PlayerInput, observer connections) is direct client↔shard against shard host ports (k3d maps 10000-10099 TCP+UDP via hostNetwork pods). The gateway never proxies game traffic and is not on the hot path. After the first redirect, ALL subsequent shard transfers are negotiated peer-to-peer between shards (PlayerHandoff/HandoffAccepted over QUIC) and pushed to the client as ShardRedirect/ShardHandoff over the existing primary TCP — the gateway is never consulted again. This is a clean, sound separation: the gateway is essentially a stateless login/placement service.
findings.evidence: gateway/src/main.rs:72-179 (one-shot handle_client); k8s/gateway.yaml:43-50 (NodePort 30777); dev-cluster.sh:106-108 (hostNetwork port maps); client/src/net/network.rs:539-604 (resolve_initial_addrs→connect_to_shard_full); k8s_provisioner.rs:184 (hostNetwork:true)

findings.title: Inter-shard QUIC has NO authentication and NO message-level trust boundary
findings.detail: quic_transport.rs uses self-signed certs with SkipServerVerification (accepts ANY server cert) and with_no_client_auth — by design ('all shards within trusted cluster'). The sender writes its own 8-byte ShardId as a stream header (recv_loop_sourced), which is purely self-asserted and trivially spoofable. The PlayerHandoff handler accepts h.source_shard and h.session_token straight from the payload with ZERO validation — any process that can reach a shard's QUIC port can inject a PlayerHandoff and spawn/teleport an arbitrary player. The AuthorizedPeers filter exists but only gates scene-data messages (SystemSceneUpdate, ShipColliderSync), NOT the handoff control plane. For a public MMO this is a critical trust gap; for the current single-tenant dev cluster it is acceptable but must be designed-in before any rebuild.
findings.evidence: quic_transport.rs:379-438 (SkipServerVerification), :318-346 (self-asserted ShardId header); harness.rs:697 (sender writes own id); system-shard/src/main.rs:863-869 (handoff accepted unvalidated); ship-shard/src/main.rs:1125-1140,1628 (AuthorizedPeers gates only scene data)

findings.title: Handoff orchestration logic is deeply embedded in 7k-9k-line shard main.rs files, not in shard-common
findings.detail: shard-common only holds the MECHANISM: handoff_pipeline.rs (145 LOC: send_handoff, send_handoff_accepted, build_post_handoff_redirect) and the ClientRegistry observer-promotion primitives (client_listener.rs:1158). The actual POLICY — which target shard to hand off to, when, EVA-exit vs hull-entry vs warp vs planet-descent routing, ShardPreConnect fan-out — lives inline in system-shard/main.rs (7328 LOC), ship-shard/main.rs (9657 LOC), planet-shard/main.rs (3714 LOC) and galaxy-shard/main.rs (1413). 349 lines across these mains mention 'handoff' directly, each shard re-implementing the PlayerHandoff/HandoffAccepted match arms and target selection. This is the core reason transfers are 'chronically broken and hard to fix': the transfer state machine is smeared across four giant binaries with per-shard-pair special cases rather than centralized.
findings.evidence: shard-common/src/handoff_pipeline.rs (145 LOC mechanism only); grep handoff counts: system-shard 45, ship-shard 35, planet-shard 16 hits; 349 total handoff-mentioning lines in mains; system-shard/main.rs:2206 comment 'same idiom as the ship-shard PlayerHandoff handler' (copy-paste coupling)

findings.title: The observer-promotion seamless-handoff model is a fragile 4-way distributed dance with documented race landmines
findings.detail: The seamless ShardHandoff path (T0 series) requires: (1) client pre-opens an observer TCP+UDP to the destination shard via ObserverConnect carrying the player's session_token; (2) destination registers it in ClientRegistry.session_observers keyed by that token; (3) on PlayerHandoff the destination calls promote_observer_to_client to move the TCP write-half in place; (4) source demotes its primary after source_demote_after_ticks (15). client_listener.rs is saturated with multi-paragraph comments documenting races this created: register-before-send ordering (else duplicate player + frozen camera), UDP-IP-match heuristic that breaks on shared IP/localhost, double-broadcast to same addr, promoted-client never reaped on EOF (ghost accumulation), bind_udp_to_session scrubbing the wrong session mid-handoff. Each fix is a point-patch. The model couples client connection lifecycle, server registry state, and UDP hole-punch discovery across two shards and one client — the combinatorial state space is the fragility source, not any single bug.
findings.evidence: client_listener.rs:199-422 (session_observers, promote_observer_to_client, bind_udp_to_session, discover_udp — ~220 lines of race-comment-laden code); client/src/net/connection.rs:425-489 (client-side promote/observer hole-punch comments); commit 5b78136 'Not fully working shard transfers', 311e66f/5275692/fe2fdcf (T0 series)

findings.title: Eviction landmine confirmed: cross-shard visibility depends on PeerShardRegistry presence; observer/UDP entries time out at 10s with no handoff-aware protection
findings.detail: OBSERVER_TIMEOUT is a hard 10s in client_listener.rs — observers (the dual-shard compositing connections) are reaped purely on last-successful-send, with no awareness of an in-flight handoff. cleanup_stale_observers runs on every broadcast. Separately, PeerShardRegistry.update() clears and rebuilds from the orchestrator every 2s, dropping any shard in Stopped/Draining; system-shard explicitly documents NOT evicting on registry-absence because 'PeerShardRegistry deletes a peer immediately on registry-lag ABSENCE' would re-introduce the bug. So cross-shard rendering and handoff targeting both ride on caches (2s peer refresh, 10s observer timeout) that can evict a still-needed peer/observer mid-transition. The QUIC dispatcher's on-demand refresh-on-cache-miss (harness.rs:591-619) is a band-aid over this same fragility.
findings.evidence: client_listener.rs:123 (OBSERVER_TIMEOUT 10s), :528-536 (cleanup_stale_observers); peer_registry.rs:38-46 (update clears all, drops Stopped/Draining); system-shard/main.rs:6267-6273 (evict_stale_surface_players comment rejecting immediate eviction); harness.rs:543-619 (on-demand refresh band-aid)

findings.title: Orchestrator + registry + provisioner is solid, well-tested, and cleanly separable from game logic
findings.detail: The orchestrator (2295 LOC) is the strongest component. registry.rs (445) maintains in-memory HashMap + planet/system/galaxy/ship indices backed by redb, with state-transition validation and full unit tests. persistence.rs (157) is a clean redb wrapper (two tables: shards, launch_configs as JSON) with roundtrip tests. lifecycle.rs (248) does dead-shard detection (heartbeat timeout), rate-limited auto-restart, and idle shutdown, with tests. provisioner.rs (101) abstracts LocalProvisioner (child procs) vs KubernetesProvisioner (327, pod-per-shard, port-pool of 4 ports/shard, per-worktree image tags) behind one trait. http_api.rs (443) is a clean axum REST surface (/register, /shards, /shard/:id, /planet,/system,/galaxy,/ship lookups with provision-on-demand + wait_for_ready). This layer knows nothing about voxels, physics, or handoffs — it only tracks ShardInfo. It is the most rebuild-survivable piece.
findings.evidence: orchestrator/src/registry.rs (445 LOC, 7 tests), persistence.rs (157, 2 tests), lifecycle.rs (248, 2 tests), provisioner.rs (101), k8s_provisioner.rs (327, 2 tests), http_api.rs (443); orchestrator/tests/http_api_test.rs (293 LOC)

findings.title: Orchestrator persists only shard topology, not session/player/transfer state — single point of failure with no HA
findings.detail: redb stores exactly two things: ShardInfo (id, type, state, endpoints, seeds, host_shard_id) and LaunchConfig (binary, args, type), both as serde_json blobs. On restart, all shards are marked Provisioning and must re-register via heartbeat. The universe_epoch_ms (the deterministic-time anchor) is NOT persisted — it resets to orchestrator start time every restart (main.rs:62 'resets each dev cycle'), which would desync celestial time across a restart. Gateway SessionStore is in-memory only (session.rs:18-19 'For production this would be backed by redb') keyed by player_name, lost on gateway restart. Orchestrator is replicas:1, strategy Recreate — a hard SPOF. No session/player-position persistence exists anywhere; player state lives only inside shard process memory and the in-flight PlayerHandoff blob. A shard crash loses all its players' positions.
findings.evidence: persistence.rs:6-7 (only 2 tables), :29 (serde_json blobs); main.rs:58-66 (epoch not persisted, resets); gateway/src/session.rs:18-19 (in-memory SessionStore); k8s/orchestrator.yaml:7-9 (replicas:1, Recreate)

findings.title: QUIC transport layer is genuinely well-engineered — persistent streams, per-peer circuit breakers, on-demand discovery
findings.detail: quic_transport.rs (451) + the per-peer send dispatcher in harness.rs (543-740) implement the 'AAA MMO pattern': each peer owns an isolated async task with its own connection, send-stream reuse, and CircuitBreaker (circuit_breaker.rs:165, exponential backoff 5s→60s, half-open recovery, fully unit-tested), so one dead peer's 2s timeout blocks only its own task, not the shared loop. recv_loop_sourced reads a per-stream ShardId header. MAX_MESSAGE_SIZE was raised 64KB→4MB to fit ShipColliderSync. The dispatcher resolves addresses lazily from PeerShardRegistry with on-demand orchestrator refresh on cache-miss (closes a documented 10s blackout for freshly-provisioned ship/planet shards). This mechanism is mature and worth keeping; the weakness is auth (separate finding), not engineering quality. circuit_breaker.rs and quic_transport.rs are the cleanest salvage candidates.
findings.evidence: quic_transport.rs:114-181 (send w/ breaker), :284-346 (recv loops); harness.rs:543-740 (per-peer isolated tasks); circuit_breaker.rs:1-165 (5 tests); quic_transport.rs:22-30 (4MB raise rationale)

findings.title: Duplicate/parallel type definitions: voxeldust-types vs core::shard_types, and orphan crates (protocol, voxydust, voxydust-next)
findings.detail: types/src/shard.rs defines ShardInfo/ShardId/etc and core/src/shard_types.rs does 'pub use voxeldust_types::shard::*' — so core RE-EXPORTS types, meaning the active path is types→core→everyone (not a true duplicate, but the indirection is confusing and types/ is one of the 'newer' crates mid-migration). Separately the repo carries both protocol/ and protocol-fb/ (two protocol crates), and three client dirs: client/ (the active bevy_ecs net stack), voxydust/, and voxydust-next/ — strongly suggesting an incomplete migration with dead/legacy code. signal/ is a newer extracted crate. This crate sprawl raises the question of which is canonical and inflates the '148k lines' figure; a rebuild should consolidate to one types crate and one client.
findings.evidence: core/src/shard_types.rs:10 (pub use voxeldust_types::shard::*); workspace members include types, protocol-fb, signal, plus root dirs protocol/, voxydust/, voxydust-next/, client/; types/Cargo.toml (voxeldust-types)

findings.title: Zero integration/e2e test coverage for the actual transfer flow
findings.detail: e2e-tests/ contains only orchestrator_api.rs (tests the REST surface). shard-common/tests covers quic_integration, chat_flow, media, antenna_terminal, metrics — but NOTHING exercises PlayerHandoff→HandoffAccepted→observer-promote→demote end to end, the ShardRedirect-vs-ShardHandoff branch, or the eviction/race scenarios the code comments describe at length. The handoff_pipeline.rs and authorized_peers.rs modules have no tests at all. Given the transfer logic is the chronically-broken part, the complete absence of automated regression coverage for it is why each manual fix regresses something else. This is a 'missing tests' problem layered on top of the architectural one.
findings.evidence: e2e-tests/tests/ = {orchestrator_api.rs} only; shard-common/tests = {antenna_terminal_e2e, chat_flow_e2e, media_e2e, metrics_integration, quic_integration} — no handoff test; handoff_pipeline.rs & authorized_peers.rs have no #[cfg(test)]

findings.title: Heartbeat/discovery design is simple and adequate but couples liveness to a 2s UDP+10s-timeout loop with static metrics
findings.detail: Shards send UDP heartbeats every 2s to the orchestrator (heartbeat_sender.rs, length-prefixed ShardMsg::Heartbeat); orchestrator marks dead at heartbeat_timeout (default 10s) and transitions Provisioning/Starting→Ready on first heartbeat. BUT harness.rs:446-453 wires a STATIC metrics closure returning (0,0,0,0) — player_count is always 0, so the orchestrator's idle-shutdown logic (0 players too long → kill) would reap EVERY shard if idle_shutdown_secs weren't bumped to 3600 in the k8s manifest. The metrics_fn is a TODO ('will be wired to tick loop later'). So idle-shutdown and player-count-based scaling are effectively non-functional; the system relies on the 1hr timeout as a safety net. Discovery itself (HTTP /shards poll every 2s into PeerShardRegistry) is fine.
findings.evidence: heartbeat_sender.rs:41-78 (2s UDP); harness.rs:446-449 (static (0.0,0.0,0,0) metrics, 'will be wired later'); k8s/orchestrator.yaml:33 (idle-shutdown-secs=3600 workaround); lifecycle.rs:65-72,154-160 (idle logic keyed on player_count)

findings.title: Two parallel QUIC send paths and a TCP-message-size cap mismatch create latent inconsistency
findings.detail: QuicTransport::send (quic_transport.rs:114) implements a full send path with shared peers Mutex + circuit breaker, but harness.rs's actual dispatcher (line 563+) RE-IMPLEMENTS the same logic per-peer (own connection, own breaker, own stream) and binds a SECOND QUIC endpoint ('0.0.0.0:0') just for sending — so the QuicTransport::send method is largely dead for shards (used by tests/handoff_pipeline which calls transport.send). Two implementations of the same protocol drift over time (the 4MB raise applies to QuicTransport but the harness dispatcher has its own copy of the read/write framing). Also TCP client messages are capped at 65536 (client_listener.rs:644,882) while QUIC allows 4MB — a ShipColliderSync-sized payload that works shard-to-shard would be rejected client-to-shard, an asymmetry worth noting for any unified protocol.
findings.evidence: quic_transport.rs:114-248 (QuicTransport::send path); harness.rs:563-740 (parallel re-implementation, second endpoint bind :565); handoff_pipeline.rs:50-54 (uses transport.send); client_listener.rs:644,882 (65536 TCP cap) vs quic_transport.rs:30 (4MB)

findings.title: ShardRedirect vs ShardHandoff branch is the right abstraction and is centralized in one helper
findings.detail: build_post_handoff_redirect (handoff_pipeline.rs:89-125) is the single source of truth for the seamless-vs-legacy decision: observer_promoted=true → ShardHandoff (zero-RTT in-place promote), else → ShardRedirect (fresh TCP handshake fallback). The doc comment explicitly notes every per-shard consumer routes through here so the invariant 'observer_promoted ⇒ ShardHandoff' can't regress in one shard only. This is a good pattern and a salvageable seam — the fallback ShardRedirect path also means the system degrades to a working (if laggy) transfer when the observer pre-connect didn't happen, which is valuable resilience. The problem is everything AROUND this helper (when/whom to hand off, observer lifecycle), not the helper itself.
findings.evidence: handoff_pipeline.rs:89-125 (build_post_handoff_redirect single decision point); planet-shard/main.rs:1841, system-shard/main.rs:514 (consumers route through it); client/src/net/network.rs:353-403 (ShardRedirect fallback), :404-469 (ShardHandoff promote)

summary:
The multi-shard infrastructure has a clean macro-architecture but a fragile transfer micro-architecture. CONNECTION FLOW: client → gateway (one-shot TCP, returns ShardRedirect, then closes) → direct client↔shard for all gameplay (TCP control + UDP WorldState/PlayerInput). The gateway is a stateless login/placement service never on the hot path. Shards self-register with the orchestrator over HTTP, heartbeat over UDP (2s), and discover peers by polling /shards into a 2s-refreshed PeerShardRegistry cache. K8s provisioning is pod-per-shard with hostNetwork and a 4-ports-per-shard pool; shards are provisioned on demand by the orchestrator's REST handlers. CONTROL PLANE = HTTP (orchestrator) + QUIC PlayerHandoff/HandoffAccepted (shard↔shard); DATA PLANE = UDP (client) + QUIC scene-sync (shard↔shard).

SEPARABILITY: The orchestrator/registry/provisioner/persistence layer (2295 LOC) and the QUIC transport + circuit breaker (quic_transport.rs, circuit_breaker.rs, peer_registry.rs, heartbeat_sender.rs) are well-engineered, tested, game-logic-agnostic, and KEEP-AND-HARDEN candidates. They know nothing about voxels or handoffs. The gateway is similarly clean and reusable.

WHY TRANSFERS ARE FRAGILE (rebuild-the-transfer-layer candidates): (1) The transfer state machine is NOT in shard-common — it is smeared across four 1.4k-9.7k-line shard main.rs files (349 handoff-mentioning lines, copy-pasted match arms). shard-common only holds the mechanism (handoff_pipeline.rs, 145 LOC). (2) The seamless observer-promotion model is a 4-way distributed dance (client observer pre-connect + dest registry promote + source demote-after-15-ticks) whose combinatorial state space generates the documented races (UDP-IP heuristics, ghost reaping, double-broadcast, register-before-send ordering). (3) The eviction landmine is real: cross-shard visibility rides on a 10s observer timeout and a 2s peer-cache that drop still-needed entries mid-transition. (4) ZERO integration tests cover the handoff flow. (5) Inter-shard QUIC has NO auth — PlayerHandoff is accepted unvalidated and spoofable.

VERDICT: Keep the orchestrator/transport/gateway substrate; REBUILD the transfer state machine transfer-first as a centralized, tested, auth-bearing protocol in shard-common rather than per-shard inline logic.</summary>
<parameter name="rebuild_implications">KEEP-AND-HARDEN (the infrastructure substrate is sound and separable from game logic): orchestrator crate (registry/lifecycle/provisioner/k8s_provisioner/http_api/persistence — 2295 LOC, well-tested, voxel-agnostic), QUIC transport (quic_transport.rs + circuit_breaker.rs + peer_registry.rs + heartbeat_sender.rs), the gateway (one-shot redirect, clean), and the harness skeleton's networking-task wiring. These can be lifted almost as-is. REBUILD TRANSFER-FIRST (this is where the chronic breakage lives): the handoff state machine must move OUT of the four giant shard main.rs files into a centralized, exhaustively-tested module in shard-common that owns the full PlayerHandoff→HandoffAccepted→promote/demote lifecycle as one explicit state machine with one set of race-free invariants, not per-shard-pair copy-paste. Before rebuilding, decide on the seamless model: the observer-promotion / dual-shard-compositing approach is the root of most races — a transfer-first foundation should treat 'seamless zero-RTT' as an optimization layered on a provably-correct ShardRedirect baseline, with integration tests gating every state transition. HARDEN REGARDLESS: add inter-shard QUIC authentication (the ShardId header is self-asserted/spoofable and PlayerHandoff is unvalidated), persist session+player-position state (currently only in shard process memory — a crash loses players), persist universe_epoch_ms, wire real heartbeat metrics (player_count is hardcoded 0), and make handoff-aware the 10s observer timeout + 2s peer cache that currently evict mid-transition. CONSOLIDATE: collapse the duplicate type/protocol/client crates (types vs core::shard_types re-export, protocol vs protocol-fb, client vs voxydust vs voxydust-next) which inflate LOC and obscure the canonical path.</parameter>
<parameter name="salvageable">["orchestrator crate end-to-end (registry.rs, lifecycle.rs, provisioner.rs, k8s_provisioner.rs, http_api.rs, persistence.rs) — game-logic-agnostic, unit-tested, the strongest piece","shard-common/src/quic_transport.rs — persistent-stream QUIC with length framing and source-ID headers (add auth before reuse)","shard-common/src/circuit_breaker.rs — clean, fully unit-tested exponential-backoff breaker with half-open recovery","shard-common/src/peer_registry.rs — simple discovery cache; the radio_fanout decision logic is reusable","shard-common/src/heartbeat_sender.rs + orchestrator/src/heartbeat.rs — minimal UDP liveness protocol","gateway crate — stateless login/placement redirect; keep the gateway→orchestrator→ShardRedirect pattern","shard-common/src/handoff_pipeline.rs build_post_handoff_redirect — the centralized ShardRedirect-vs-ShardHandoff decision is the right seam to build a new transfer state machine around","k8s manifests + dev-cluster.sh worktree-slot tooling — pragmatic per-agent cluster isolation, reusable as-is","The harness NetworkBridge / per-peer QUIC dispatcher pattern (concept, not the duplicated impl) — isolating each peer in its own task is the correct model"]
open_questions: Is the seamless observer-promotion model (dual-shard compositing) a hard product requirement, or is a ~50ms ShardRedirect handshake gap acceptable? This determines whether the entire session_observers/promote machinery (the main race source) can be deleted in a rebuild.
Which client is canonical — client/ vs voxydust/ vs voxydust-next/ — and can the other two be deleted? Same for protocol/ vs protocol-fb/.

Is there any intent to run multiple orchestrator replicas / multi-region shards? Current design is replicas:1 SPOF with in-memory gateway sessions — a transfer-first foundation may need durable session+position state and HA from the start.
What is the threat model for inter-shard QUIC? If shards will ever run across trust boundaries (multi-tenant, player-hosted), the no-auth/spoofable-ShardId design needs replacing, not hardening.

Does player state need to survive a shard crash? Today positions live only in shard process memory and the in-flight handoff blob — nothing is persisted, so a crashed shard loses all its players' positions.
